questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The Michaelis constant Km represents:
options: The substrate concentration at half maximal velocity, inversely related to enzyme affinity
questions.concept: A low Km indicates high affinity. Hexokinase has a low Km working at all glucose levels, while glucokinase in the liver has a high Km, acting only when glucose is abundant after a meal.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor characteristically:
options: Increases Km without changing Vmax, and can be overcome by excess substrate
questions.concept: Non-competitive inhibitors reduce Vmax with unchanged Km. Ethanol competitively inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase is the therapeutic basis of treating methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Allosteric enzymes characteristically show:
options: Sigmoid kinetics with regulation at a site distinct from the active site
questions.concept: Phosphofructokinase-1 is the key allosteric regulator and rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The cardiac biomarker of choice for diagnosing myocardial infarction is:
options: Troponin I or T, which rise within 3 to 4 hours and remain elevated for days
questions.concept: Troponins are the most sensitive and specific. CK-MB, normalising in 2 to 3 days, remains useful for detecting reinfarction, whereas troponin stays elevated for up to 10 days.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A markedly raised serum amylase with normal lipase suggests:
options: A non-pancreatic cause such as salivary disease, perforation or macroamylasaemia
questions.concept: Lipase is more specific and remains elevated longer than amylase. Neither enzyme level correlates with severity of pancreatitis, which is assessed clinically and radiologically.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A raised alkaline phosphatase with a raised gamma-glutamyl transferase indicates:
options: A hepatobiliary rather than bony source
questions.concept: GGT confirms hepatic origin, while a raised ALP with normal GGT suggests bone disease, growing children or pregnancy. This simple pairing localises the source without isoenzyme studies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: An AST to ALT ratio greater than 2 is characteristic of:
questions.concept: ALT is more liver-specific and predominates in viral hepatitis. The alcoholic pattern reflects pyridoxine deficiency impairing ALT synthesis and mitochondrial injury releasing AST.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Isoenzymes are best defined as:
options: Different molecular forms of an enzyme catalysing the same reaction, often tissue-specific
questions.concept: Lactate dehydrogenase has five isoenzymes: LDH1 predominates in heart and red cells, LDH5 in liver and skeletal muscle, and an LDH1 greater than LDH2 flipped pattern once indicated infarction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Zymogens (proenzymes) exist because:
options: Premature activation would digest the tissue of origin, as in acute pancreatitis
questions.concept: Trypsinogen activation within the pancreas triggers the enzymatic cascade of acute pancreatitis. Protective mechanisms include the pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor, whose failure is implicated in hereditary pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction but do not:
options: Alter the equilibrium constant or the free energy change of the reaction
questions.concept: Enzymes accelerate attainment of equilibrium in both directions equally. The thermodynamic favourability is fixed by the reactants, which is why an enzyme cannot make an endergonic reaction spontaneous.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The end product of purine catabolism in humans is:
questions.concept: Humans lack uricase, so urate is the end product and its low solubility predisposes to gout and urate stones. Most other mammals convert it further to soluble allantoin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of de novo purine synthesis is:
questions.concept: It is feedback-inhibited by AMP, GMP and IMP. The salvage pathway using HGPRT is far more energy-efficient, and its complete absence causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome results from deficiency of:
options: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase, inherited as X-linked recessive
questions.concept: Loss of purine salvage causes hyperuricaemia with gout, intellectual disability, choreoathetosis, spasticity and compulsive self-mutilation. Allopurinol controls the urate but not the neurological features.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Allopurinol lowers uric acid by inhibiting:
questions.concept: Blocking conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to urate reduces production. The accumulated precursors are more soluble and readily excreted, which is why xanthine stones are rare.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes:
options: Severe combined immunodeficiency from accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine in lymphocytes
questions.concept: dATP accumulation inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, halting DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes. It was the first disease treated by gene therapy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Orotic aciduria is a defect of:
options: Pyrimidine synthesis, causing megaloblastic anaemia unresponsive to B12 or folate
questions.concept: Deficiency of UMP synthase causes orotic acid excretion with megaloblastic anaemia and failure to thrive, treated with uridine which bypasses the block. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency also raises orotate but with hyperammonaemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Methotrexate inhibits nucleotide synthesis by blocking:
options: Dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidylate synthesis
questions.concept: 5-fluorouracil instead inhibits thymidylate synthase directly. Both cause a thymineless death in rapidly dividing cells, explaining their myelosuppression and mucositis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Secondary hyperuricaemia in a patient starting chemotherapy for leukaemia results from:
options: Tumour lysis syndrome releasing nucleic acids for purine catabolism
questions.concept: Massive cell lysis causes hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia with acute kidney injury. Hydration with allopurinol or rasburicase is given prophylactically.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Ribonucleotide reductase is important because it:
options: Converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, the committed step for DNA synthesis
questions.concept: Hydroxyurea inhibits it, which is why hydroxyurea is used in myeloproliferative disease and sickle cell disease, where it also raises fetal haemoglobin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Uric acid stones are radiolucent and are managed by:
options: Urinary alkalinisation with high fluid intake and allopurinol
questions.concept: Urate is far more soluble at alkaline pH, so potassium citrate can dissolve existing stones - one of the few stone types amenable to medical dissolution. They are invisible on plain radiograph but seen on CT.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of haem synthesis is:
options: ALA synthase, inhibited by haem through feedback
questions.concept: Drugs that induce cytochrome P450 consume haem, de-repressing ALA synthase and precipitating acute porphyric attacks - the mechanism behind barbiturate, phenytoin and sulphonamide triggers.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Lead poisoning inhibits which enzymes of haem synthesis?
questions.concept: The block causes microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and raised free erythrocyte protoporphyrin and urinary ALA, alongside abdominal colic, a gum lead line and peripheral neuropathy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Acute intermittent porphyria presents with:
options: Abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric features and dark urine, without photosensitivity
questions.concept: Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes attacks precipitated by drugs, fasting, alcohol and infection. Because the defect is proximal to photosensitising porphyrinogens, skin is spared, unlike cutaneous porphyrias.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Acute porphyric attacks are treated with:
options: Intravenous glucose and haem arginate, which suppress ALA synthase
questions.concept: High carbohydrate intake and haem provide negative feedback. Barbiturates, sulphonamides, phenytoin, oestrogens and alcohol are all contraindicated as enzyme inducers.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Unconjugated bilirubin differs from conjugated in that it is:
options: Water insoluble, albumin bound and does not appear in urine
questions.concept: Being lipid soluble, unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier causing kernicterus in neonates. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and appears in urine, giving dark urine in obstructive jaundice.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Bilirubin is conjugated in the liver by:
questions.concept: Deficiency causes Gilbert syndrome with mild fluctuating unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia worsened by fasting and stress, and Crigler-Najjar syndrome in its severe form. Phenobarbitone induces the enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: In haemolytic jaundice, the urine characteristically shows:
questions.concept: Unconjugated bilirubin cannot be filtered, so urine bilirubin is absent - the acholuric jaundice of haemolysis - while increased gut conversion raises urobilinogen. Obstructive jaundice shows the reverse pattern.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is characterised by:
options: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a black pigmented liver from impaired canalicular excretion
questions.concept: A defect in the MRP2 canalicular transporter causes benign conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Rotor syndrome is similar but without hepatic pigmentation, and both have an excellent prognosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Phototherapy for neonatal jaundice works by:
options: Converting bilirubin to water-soluble lumirubin and photoisomers excretable without conjugation
questions.concept: Blue light at 450 nm is most effective. Exchange transfusion is reserved for very high levels or signs of encephalopathy, and immunoglobulin is used in isoimmune haemolytic disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Physiological jaundice of the newborn is explained by:
options: Immature glucuronyl transferase with increased red cell breakdown and enterohepatic recycling
questions.concept: It appears after 24 hours, peaks at day 3 to 5 and resolves within 2 weeks. Jaundice within 24 hours, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, or persistence beyond 2 weeks is always pathological.
